newsitem.title: PERU: Peru withdraws envoy from Uruguay after siege swap.
newsitem.headline: Peru withdraws envoy from Uruguay after siege swap.

text.p: Peru recalled its top diplomat in Uruguay on Wednesday after Uruguay freed two alleged Peruvian guerrillas and secured the release of its ambassador in the Lima hostage crisis.
"We can confirm we have withdrawn the chief of mission of Peru in Uruguay," a Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.

The official, who asked not to be named, would not comment on the reason for the withdrawal of Efrain Saavedra, deputy head of mission who was in charge of the embassy in Montevideo in the absence of the ambassador.

Peru's decision appeared to be a protest at Tuesday's release by Uruguay of two alleged members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), which is holding 105 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori has firmly refused to give in to the demands of rebels, who are seeking the release of some 400 jailed comrades since they stormed the Japanese diplomatic reception a week ago.

Peruvians were angered by the surprise release on Tuesday of Uruguay's ambassador, Tabare Bocalandro, only hours after his country overruled a Peruvian extradition request for a man and woman believed to belong to the MRTA and set them free.
While other Latin American diplomats had been freed by the hostage-takers, Bocalandro had apparently been held on as a bargaining chip to press Uruguay to release the two comrades.
Uruguay denied it had negotiated a swap, but a well-placed Uruguayan government source told Reuters a deal was struck.
Uruguayan officials said the run-in did not threaten diplomatic ties between the two South American nations.
"For the time being we should not think of a break in relations," Uruguay's Foreign Minister Alvaro Ramos told a local radio station.
A Uruguayan appeals court freed Luis Alberto Samaniego and Silvia Gora Rivera, who were arrested in Uruguay a year ago in connection with the 1995 kidnapping of a Bolivian businessman.
The ruling revoked an earlier court decision to authorise their extradition to Peru. Samaniego and Gora had appealed on the grounds that they would not get a fair trial in Peru.

The couple were arrested entering Uruguay with false Bolivian documents in 1995. They were suspected of taking part in the MRTA kidnapping of Bolivian businessman and former government official Samuel Doria Medina, who was freed a month and a half later after a $1.2 million ransom was paid.
Uruguayan media speculated on Wednesday that Samaniego and Gora had arrived in Montevideo to collect the rasom.
